answer.question: What was the Kubernetes release cadence before 2021?
answer.answer: Historically Kubernetes followed a four-releases-per-calendar-year cadence, roughly one minor release per quarter. 2020 was the exception. The three-releases-per-year cadence was then made official on April 23, 2021, starting with the 1.22 release.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes move to three releases per year?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes moved from four releases a year (once a quarter) to three. The change was made official by a KEP merged on April 23, 2021. The evidence gives several reasons:

- **Growing burden from bigger releases.** As the project matured, each cycle carried more enhancements. That put more load on contributors and the Release Engineering team. Downstream consumers and integrators also struggled to keep up with ever more feature-packed releases, and wider adoption meant a longer chain of consumers affected.
- **The pandemic and user feedback.** The 1.19 cycle was extended because of COVID-19, and 1.20 became the third and final release of 2020. The release team also said it had listened to users about how many releases there should be each year.
- **End users couldn't keep pace.** Most organizations found it hard to do a minor upgrade every 3 months, or they fell out of security support within a year. More frequent releases only lower risk if users can actually apply the upgrades. With fewer releases, users spend less time upgrading. Each release is also supported a bit longer, so bug fixes and security patches stay available longer. This is not strictly an LTS policy.
- **Contributors and enhancements.** Contributors get more time to mature enhancements and get them ready for production.
- **SIG Release overhead.** SIG Release has less management overhead and fewer overlapping patch-release branches to maintain (3 instead of up to 4). It gets more time for smooth handovers between release teams and can take on more shadows. Freed time can go into release quality and tooling.
- **Predictability and risk.** Three releases leave more room for triage, development, conferences and cycle preparation. That should mean better planning, more predictability and lower overall risk.

The trade-off is slower feature graduation: going from alpha to stable stretches from 9 to 12 months. Each release also contains more enhancements.

answer.question: What enforces pod security standards in-tree?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes enforces the Pod Security Standards in-tree with its built-in Pod Security admission controller (PodSecurity). It intercepts requests in the API server before they are persisted and admits or denies them. It applies restrictions at the namespace level when pods are created, checking each pod spec against the configured Pod Security Standard. You can configure it with cluster-wide defaults and exemptions. It is also meant to replace the deprecated PodSecurityPolicies.

Its maturity by release:
- v1.22: it first appeared as alpha, and you had to enable the `PodSecurity` feature gate.
- v1.23: it graduated to beta. The docs for 1.23–1.25 still say to make sure the feature gate is enabled.
- v1.25: it became stable.

The same logic can also run outside the API server as a standalone webhook.

answer.question: What were Pod Security Admission's graduation stages?
answer.answer:
Pod Security Admission, controlled by the `PodSecurity` feature gate, went through three stages:

- **Alpha in v1.22.** It was off by default, both the feature gate and the built-in admission controller. Initial E2E feature tests ran in an alpha test job. The alpha was released on 2021-08-04.
- **Beta in v1.23–1.24.** It was on by default, and the admission plugin was added to the default enabled set. Enforcement still had to be turned on per namespace. To reach beta, the project had to settle several open items: restricted-policy support for Windows pods, the deprecation policy for old profile versions, ephemeral containers support, and PSP migration. The beta was released on 2021-11-03.
- **GA (stable) in v1.25.** The GA target had earlier been planned as v1.24, so that users could migrate off PodSecurityPolicy before it was removed in v1.25. GA added the `pod-security.admission.config.k8s.io/v1` admission configuration, unchanged from v1beta1, and some user-experience improvements.

The feature gate stayed stable through v1.27 and was later removed.

heading_path: What does this mean for you?

answer.question: Why was PodSecurityPolicy replaced instead of fixed?
answer.answer:
PodSecurityPolicy had serious usability problems that couldn't be fixed without breaking changes, so it was deprecated (as of v1.21) instead of being promoted to GA. The problems fell into three groups:

1. **Policy authorization model.** Policies were bound either to the requesting user or to the pod's service account. Granting permission to the user is intuitive but breaks controllers, and the dual model weakens security. How PSPs applied to Pods confused nearly everyone. It was easy to grant broader permissions than intended and hard to inspect which PSP applied.
2. **Rollout challenges.** PSP fails closed when no policy exists, so it could never be enabled by default. It needed 100% coverage before rollout and had no dry-run or audit mode, which made it impractical to retrofit safely onto existing clusters.
3. **Inconsistent and unbounded API.** The API grew organically and has many internal inconsistencies. It was unclear what belonged in PSP, it didn't compose well, and mutation priority or changed Pod defaults could behave unexpectedly.

The project still wanted a built-in way to stop privilege escalation through the create-pod permission. So it built a new, simpler admission controller (KEP-2579, now Pod Security admission). The replacement draws on these lessons:
- It has soft rollout features so it can be retrofitted to existing clusters.
- It is configurable enough to eventually be on by default.
- It can be partly or fully deactivated to coexist with external admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA/Gatekeeper.

PSP was removed in v1.25.

answer.question: What happens to unused auto-generated ServiceAccount token Secrets?
answer.answer:
Since Kubernetes 1.29, auto-generated legacy ServiceAccount token Secrets that sit unused are first marked invalid and later deleted. An auto-generated token is one that is bi-directionally referenced by a ServiceAccount, meaning it is listed in the ServiceAccount's `secrets` field.

The legacy ServiceAccount token cleaner runs in kube-controller-manager and checks every 24 hours. It first looks at the tracking ConfigMap (`kube-apiserver-legacy-service-account-token-tracking`). If that ConfigMap is unavailable, nothing is removed. Otherwise it evaluates each Secret of type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token`.

The cleaner marks a Secret invalid only if all of these are true:
- It is auto-generated.
- It is not mounted by any pod.
- It has not been used for the clean-up period since it was created or last used.

To work out when a token was last used, the cleaner reads the `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-last-used` label. If that label is missing, or is older than the tracking date (`since`) in the ConfigMap, it uses that `since` date instead.

Marking a Secret invalid means adding the label `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-invalid-since` with the current date. If someone then uses the invalidated token, the validator:
- adds the audit annotation `authentication.k8s.io/legacy-token-invalidated: <secret name>/<namespace>`,
- increments the `invalid_legacy_auto_token_uses_total` metric,
- updates the `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-last-used` label,
- returns an error saying the token has been invalidated.

Users can remove the `invalid-since` label to temporarily re-allow the token, or switch to the TokenRequest API. If an invalidated Secret stays unused for another clean-up period, the cleaner deletes it.

The clean-up period defaults to one year. Administrators can change it with the `--legacy-service-account-token-clean-up-period` flag on kube-controller-manager.

Earlier designs (KEP versions before 1.28) proposed deleting such secrets directly after the period, with no invalidation step.

answer.question: Did Kubernetes create a token Secret for every ServiceAccount?
answer.answer: Yes, historically. Before version 1.24, Kubernetes automatically generated Secret-based tokens for ServiceAccounts. Such an auto-generated legacy token is the Secret listed in the ServiceAccount's `secrets` field. In 1.24 the `LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration` feature gate became beta and was enabled by default. With it, the token controller stops auto-creating Secrets, so Secret objects holding service account tokens are no longer generated for every ServiceAccount. To get tokens now, use the TokenRequest API. If you need a non-expiring token, explicitly create a Secret for the token controller to fill in; explicitly requested tokens are not deleted. Starting in 1.29, auto-generated legacy tokens that go unused for a period (one year by default) are marked invalid, and are later purged if they stay unused.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes stop auto-generating Secret-based ServiceAccount tokens?
answer.answer: Because, with BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume going GA in 1.22, pods obtain their service account tokens through the TokenRequest API and store them as projected volumes. Those tokens are time-limited and bound to specific pods. That made auto-generated Secret-based tokens unnecessary, and they are less secure than bound tokens. So the Token Controller was changed to stop auto-creating token Secrets for service accounts. This was the LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration feature: beta and on by default in 1.24, stable in 1.26. Users are pointed to the TokenRequest API, or to manually created Secret-based tokens if a non-expiring token is needed. The follow-up LegacyServiceAccountTokenCleanUp feature, beta in 1.29, marks long-unused legacy auto-generated tokens as invalid and later deletes them, to reduce the potential attack surface.

answer.question: Does the API server reject IP addresses with leading zeros by default?
answer.answer: It depends on the release. As of the current release (1.36 onward), yes. The StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate is beta and enabled by default from 1.36. With it enabled, octets within IPv4 addresses may not have leading 0s (and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values like ::ffff:192.168.0.1 are also forbidden). In 1.33–1.35 the gate was alpha and disabled by default. In those releases such values were still accepted, but the API server returned a warning that they would be rejected in the future. Before that, Kubernetes deliberately kept allowing leading zeros for compatibility, as noted in 1.23 even after Go 1.17 began rejecting them. The stricter check applies only to fields in built-in API kinds. It does not cover custom resource kinds, values in Kubernetes configuration files, or command-line arguments.

answer.question: Before strict IP validation was on by default, what happened when a Service used an IPv4 address with leading zeros?
answer.answer:
It was accepted, but the API server returned a warning. Kubernetes kept allowing leading zeros in IPv4 addresses for compatibility, even after Go 1.17's net.ParseIP and net.ParseCIDR started rejecting them. Kubernetes parsed such values as decimal by simply ignoring the extra zeros, so "012.000.001.002" became 12.0.1.2. Much libc-based code reads them as octal instead (10.0.1.2), which is the security concern behind CVE-2021-29923.

Service IP/CIDR fields have returned warnings for these values since 1.27. An example warning is: non-standard IP address "05.06.07.08" will be considered invalid in a future Kubernetes release: use "5.6.7.8".

The StrictIPCIDRValidation gate arrived in 1.33 as alpha, off by default. With it disabled, an invalid value such as a bad .spec.clusterIP is still allowed, with a warning that it will be rejected in the future. With it enabled, the value causes a validation error. The gate became beta and enabled by default in 1.36.

answer.question: What are the release stages of strict IP/CIDR validation (KEP-4858)?
answer.answer:
Strict IP/CIDR validation is controlled by the StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate.

- Alpha: introduced in Kubernetes 1.33 and remained alpha through 1.35, disabled by default (defaultValue false). The KEP's Alpha criteria were: API warnings added, mandatory strict validation for NetworkDeviceData, all kube-internal controllers writing only canonical IPs/CIDRs, the updated validation behind a feature gate but disabled by default, and unit tests added or updated.
- Beta: from Kubernetes 1.36, enabled by default (defaultValue true). The KEP's Beta criteria were: all UNRESOLVED items resolved, the updated validation enabled by default behind the gate, unit tests updated, and old e2e tests removed. The KEP required at least 3 releases between Alpha and Beta, so that components that might still write invalid values would be fixed first.
- Stable: in the 1.37+ KEP chunks, the KEP's status is listed as implemented/stable. However, the feature gate reference in the evidence (valid 1.36–now) lists only the alpha and beta stages and no GA stage or version.

When enabled, the gate forbids leading zeros in IPv4 octets and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values in built-in API kinds.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes tighten validation of IP addresses and CIDRs in API fields?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes's validation of IP and CIDR strings in API fields had historically been too lax. It accepted anything that Go's net.ParseIP and net.ParseCIDR accepted, even though some of those strings were ambiguous. Two examples are IPv4 octets with leading 0s, such as 172.030.099.099, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values like ::ffff:192.168.0.1.

Ambiguous values can cause security problems when different components read the same string as different IP addresses, as in CVE-2021-29923. After Go 1.17 changed how it handles leading-zero IPs to address that CVE, there was consensus that Kubernetes API validation should become stricter too. It was not done right away because the project didn't want to retroactively invalidate existing API objects. KEP-4858 set out the plan to finally do it.

The goal is to make ambiguously-interpretable IPs/CIDRs impossible in new objects. The rollout tries to avoid breaking existing objects and workflows:
- It was preceded by several releases of apiserver warnings.
- The stricter validation sits behind the StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate (alpha in 1.33, beta in 1.36).
- Pre-existing invalid values don't have to be fixed on unrelated updates.

The v1.36 release blog adds that the change helps catch malformed addresses that could otherwise cause confusing runtime behavior or security surprises.

answer.question: How long does a Kubernetes minor release receive patch support?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes 1.19 and newer receive approximately 1 year of patch support; 1.18 and older received about 9 months. In more detail, a patch release series is supported for roughly 14 months. The first 12 months are the standard support period. Near the end of those 12 months, Release Managers cut a release and the series enters a two-month maintenance mode. During maintenance mode, extra releases may be cut only for:
- vulnerabilities with an assigned CVE ID
- dependency issues, including base image updates
- critical core component issues

After maintenance mode ends, the series is end of life (EOL). Release branches are maintained for the three most recent minor releases.

answer.question: When were the legacy apt.kubernetes.io and yum.kubernetes.io package repositories frozen, and when were they removed?
answer.answer: The legacy Google-hosted repositories (apt.kubernetes.io and yum.kubernetes.io) were formally deprecated on August 31, 2023. Their contents were frozen on (approximately) September 13, 2023, right after the September 2023 patch releases (v1.28.2, v1.27.6, v1.26.9, v1.25.14). Those were the last releases published to both the legacy and the community-owned repositories; from October 2023 on, packages go only to pkgs.k8s.io. On January 12, 2024, Kubernetes said it intended to remove the repositories in January 2024. They were actually removed on March 4, 2024, and Kubernetes packages can no longer be installed from them. The v1.29 release post (chunk 43096) still says they "will go away entirely in January of 2024"; the March 26, 2024 update gives the actual removal date of March 4, 2024.

heading_path: Why we decided to change the release cadence
What this means for end users

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes extend patch support for minor releases from 9 months to about a year?
answer.answer:
Patch support was extended mainly because end users asked for it. Most business cycles (financial, certification, sales, vacation, HR and others) run on a yearly basis, so users wanted support that lasts at least a year. Nine months was an awkward period compared with most companies' planning, operations and budget cycles. A minor release every three months also meant users constantly had to evaluate, plan and carry out upgrades.

An early-2019 WG LTS survey showed that many users failed to upgrade within the 9-month window. About a third had production machines on versions that had already dropped out of support. The KEP estimated that a 12–14 month window would raise the share of users on supported versions from 50–60% to over 80%. It described a yearly period as giving users the cushion they wanted and fitting better with familiar annual planning.

The project saw the extension as a relatively small change that was still workable to implement. It was a meaningful first response to users that would also expose any unknowns of changing support windows.

The policy that resulted is about 14 months: roughly 12 months of standard support plus 2 months of maintenance mode as an upgrade period. This formalized the existing practice of keeping patch-branch CI running for 6–7 weeks past the 9 months, in case critical CVEs or upgrade blockers appeared. Kubernetes 1.19 was the first release to receive a year of patch support.

answer.question: How do I configure the kube-apiserver to use more than one authorization webhook?
answer.answer:
Use a structured authorization configuration file instead of the `--authorization-*` command-line flags. With the flags you can enable only one webhook in the authorization chain (via `--authorization-modes`). The structured config lets you declare the whole authorizer chain, including several webhooks, each with its own settings, in a set precedence order and with its own failure mode.

Write an `AuthorizationConfiguration` file (`apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1beta1` in current releases; `v1alpha1` in the older KEP examples). List the authorizers under `authorizers:` in the order they should be consulted. Each `type: Webhook` entry needs:
- **`name`**: required; used for metrics.
- A **`webhook`** block with:
  - `timeout` (maximum 30s).
  - `subjectAccessReviewVersion` (`v1` or `v1beta1`).
  - `matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion` (`v1`).
  - `failurePolicy`: `Deny` rejects the request without consulting later authorizers; `NoOpinion` continues to later authorizers.
  - Optional `authorizedTTL` and `unauthorizedTTL`.
  - `connectionInfo`:
    - In current docs: `type: KubeConfigFile` plus `kubeConfigFile: <path>`.
    - In the 1.30-era and KEP examples: `type: KubeConfig`.
    - `InClusterConfig` also exists but is not allowed for kube-apiserver.
  - Optional `matchConditions`: CEL expressions, up to 64. If any is false, the webhook is skipped. If all are true, it is called. If one errors, `failurePolicy` decides.

Example:
```yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationConfiguration
authorizers:
  - type: Webhook
    name: system-crd-protector
    webhook:
      unauthorizedTTL: 30s
      timeout: 3s
      subjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      failurePolicy: Deny
      connectionInfo:
        type: KubeConfigFile
        kubeConfigFile: /files/kube-system-authz-webhook.yaml
      matchConditions:
      - expression: has(request.resourceAttributes)
  - type: Node
  - type: RBAC
  - name: opa
    type: Webhook
    webhook:
      unauthorizedTTL: 30s
      timeout: 3s
      subjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      failurePolicy: Deny
      connectionInfo:
        type: KubeConfigFile
        kubeConfigFile: /files/opa-default-authz-webhook.yaml
      matchConditions:
      - expression: has(request.resourceAttributes)
      - expression: request.resourceAttributes.namespace == 'default'
```

The evidence doesn't name the kube-apiserver flag that points to this file.

answer.question: Before v1.29, could the kube-apiserver trust more than one OIDC issuer?
answer.answer:
No. Through v1.28 the kube-apiserver's built-in OIDC authenticator, configured with the `--oidc-*` flags, could trust only one issuer. The Authenticating docs for those releases say the API server "can only be configured to trust a single issuer." Admins who wanted multiple OAuth clients were pointed to identity providers that support the `azp` (authorized party) claim.

The Structured Authentication Config KEP (KEP-3331) agrees. It lists "use more than one OIDC provider" as a goal and says the only option at that point was an external OIDC provider that multiplexes multiple providers. The KEP proposes a configuration file with a list of issuers to fix this. In the KEP versions valid for 1.27–1.28 that design was still at alpha (implementable) stage.

answer.question: What were the graduation stages of KMS v2 encryption at rest?
answer.answer:
The KMSv2 feature gate (which enables the KMS v2 API for encryption at rest) went through these stages:
- Alpha in 1.25–1.26, disabled by default.
- Beta in 1.27–1.28, enabled by default.
- Stable (GA) from 1.29, enabled by default.

The gate was then removed after 1.31. From 1.32 on, the reference lists it as removed, with the stable stage running 1.29–1.31.

The KEP (KEP-3299) also set criteria for these stages:
- Beta: the feature is enabled by default, the documented tests are complete, there is a pkcs11 reference implementation, and the API server has metrics to gauge performance impact.
- GA: tracing is added to the API server, at least 2 KMSv2 plugin implementations are available, and there is a reference implementation using PKCS11.

heading_path: Migration from command line arguments to configuration file

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes add a structured authentication configuration file instead of keeping the --oidc-* flags?
answer.answer:
According to KEP-3331, SIG Auth wanted to move away from a flag-based OIDC configuration that kept growing without bounds and replace it with a proper, versioned config format. The new format would make it easier to support features users had asked for:
- multiple client IDs
- identifying users by more than one JWT claim
- mapping any ID-token claim into user info extra attributes
- failing authentication unless the user belongs to specific groups
- array support in required claims
- forwarding audiences to authorization

The KEP's goals list several things the flags could not provide:
- Flexible claim validation rules. The existing provider only validated the audience claim, and only by exact value.
- Richer claim mappings, including nested claims. The flags could only pick a single value from a single claim and prefix groups.
- More than one OIDC provider without relying on an external multiplexing provider.
- Changing authenticator settings without restarting kube-apiserver.
- Validation rules on the final user info object.
- Easy migration from the existing flags.

The 1.30 beta blog post adds that SIG Auth recommends the file-based approach because it gives more flexibility and extensibility. The command-line options still work for backward compatibility. However, `--authentication-config` cannot be combined with `--oidc-*` flags: if both are set, the API server reports an error and exits.

answer.question: Is kube-proxy's ipvs mode still supported, and what should I use instead?
answer.answer: Yes, but it is deprecated. kube-proxy's ipvs mode was deprecated in v1.35 and is still available, but kube-proxy logs a deprecation warning at startup when it is configured to use it. It is Linux-only. Under the current plan, a `KubeProxyIPVS` feature gate (added in v1.37, enabled by default) controls it. From v1.40 ipvs mode is expected to be disabled by default, though you can turn it back on with that feature gate. In v1.43 it is to be removed entirely. Instead, use the `nftables` proxy mode on Linux nodes. It is the recommended replacement and performs better than both iptables and ipvs. If your Linux systems are too old to run nftables mode, consider `iptables` mode rather than `ipvs`, because iptables performance has improved greatly. To check which mode you run now: `kubectl -n kube-system get configmap kube-proxy -o jsonpath='{.data.config\.conf}' | grep 'mode:'`.

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how did you turn on IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack networking?
answer.answer:
In 1.20, dual-stack had to be switched on explicitly by enabling the `IPv6DualStack` feature gate and setting dual-stack network ranges on each component:

- **kube-apiserver:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`
- **kube-controller-manager:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`, `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`. Optionally set `--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv4` and `--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv6`, which default to /24 and /64.
- **kubelet:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`
- **kube-proxy:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`

Example CIDRs are `10.244.0.0/16` for IPv4 and the format `fdXY:IJKL:MNOP:15::/64` for IPv6.

The feature was alpha in 1.20 and had been reimplemented to support dual-stack Services. Once it was enabled, Services could use IPv4, IPv6, or both. Later, from 1.21, dual-stack was enabled by default.

answer.question: When did kube-proxy's nftables mode become generally available, and what came before?
answer.answer:
kube-proxy's nftables mode became generally available (stable) in Kubernetes v1.33. Before that, it went through two earlier stages:

- **Alpha in 1.29.** The 1.29 changelog said it passed e2e testing but had not yet seen real-world use. It was described as functionally mostly identical to iptables mode, except that it would never support NodePorts on 127.0.0.1. Its nftables-specific settings required a config file, and it had not yet been heavily optimized for performance.
- **Beta in 1.31.** It sat behind the `NFTablesProxyMode` feature gate, which was now enabled by default. It was still described as relatively new and possibly not compatible with all network plugins. It ran only on Linux nodes with kernel 5.13 or later, and some NodePort behaviours differed from iptables mode.

The KEP's implementation history lists the initial proposal on 2023-02-01, merge on 2023-10-06, beta updates on 2024-05-24 and GA updates on 2025-01-15.

Even at GA, iptables remains the default on Linux nodes for compatibility reasons. A newer KEP, KEP-5343 (still provisional), plans to make nftables the default in 1.40.

answer.question: Why did SIG Network build a new nftables backend for kube-proxy?
answer.answer: Several reasons are given in the evidence: (1) The iptables kernel subsystem has unfixable/unsolvable performance problems, and upstream Linux development has moved on from iptables to nftables (new features and performance improvements go mostly into nftables). Some Linux distributions have already started to deprecate and remove iptables, and nftables claims to solve iptables' main performance problems. (2) KEP-3866 also argues that the existing ipvs mode of kube-proxy, and the nf_tables mode of /sbin/iptables, won't solve these problems, and that the iptables mode of kube-proxy has grown crufty. (3) SIG Network currently supports both the iptables and ipvs backends. It feels it can't drop ipvs because of perceived performance issues with iptables. A new backend that is as functional and non-buggy as iptables but as performant as ipvs could eventually let them deprecate both existing backends and support only one Linux backend. (4) Writing a new mode would also help focus cleanup and refactoring of the kube-proxy library code. It also gives a chance to fix legacy iptables behaviors, for example not enabling route_localnet and adding a stricter startup mode.
